newsitem.title: USA: Cigarette smoking risk rises, especially for women.
newsitem.headline: Cigarette smoking risk rises, especially for women.

text.p: The risk of dying from smoking cigarettes has risen significantly since the first Surgeon General's report in 1964, particularly for women, the National Cancer Institute reported on Wednesday.

In a new analysis of five long-term studies on smoking and health, the institute found the risks for all smoking-related causes of death increased for both men and women -- but rose more steeply for women. The diseases included lung and other cancers, heart disease, strokes and chronic obstructive lung diseases.

Overall, before the 1964 report, about 30 percent of smokers could expect to die early because of their tobacco use, the institute's Dr. Donald Shopland said by telephone. "Now what you're seeing is a bit over half would die early because of smoking."
Where the relative risks of certain smoking-related ailments used to diverge widely between men and women, now both male and female smokers face similar chances of an early death, Shopland said.

For example, he said, men who smoke now face twice the risk of dying early from lung cancer as they did before 1964. But women smokers' risk of a lung cancer death has increased four- or five-fold, Shopland said.
The mortality risk of other smoking-related diseases has increased anywhere from 20 percent to 50 percent over the same time period.
Before the Surgeon General's first report warned of the dangers of smoking, about 40 percent of men who smoked could expect to die early, while only 18 percent of women smokers faced the same fate.
But now 57 percent of male smokers may die prematurely as a result of smoking, as compared with 48 percent of women.
The dramatic increase in risk for women may be due in part to the time when the earliest studies were conducted, Shopland said.

In the earliest of the five studies, which date from 1954 and 1959 respectively, the women included in the analysis probably smoked for a shorter time, mostly because smoking was socially less acceptable for women in the earlier parts of the 20th century, according to Shopland.
However, the later studies -- dated 1976, 1979 and 1982 -- may reflect an easing of societal pressures against women smoking.

Shopland noted that the institute's analysis dealt only with the relative risks for those who smoke, not for the overall U.S. population. He said about 25 percent of American adults smoke now, compared with about 45 percent who smoked three decades ago.
He said this analysis could be a "wake-up call" to focus more on women's health issues, especially as they relate to smoking and smoking-related ailments.
